description:
STEM ALIENS is a team of six passionate students interested in technology, science, engineering, and space exploration.

Our team combines skills in Full-Stack Development, AI/ML, Data Science, Robotics, Physics, Engineering, and UI/UX Design. We believe in turning creative ideas into practical solutions through collaboration and innovation.

We're looking to push boundaries, learn from others, and build something meaningful. 

Beyond Earth. Beyond Limits. 👽
summary:
We developed an interactive space exploration platform that combines gamification, NASA data, and AI-powered assistance to make space science more accessible, engaging, and educational.
The platform features multiple integrated AI assistant that guides the player and give hints to him throughout the game to help him make better choices.
Our solution addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific data into accessible, interactive, and meaningful experiences. Instead of simply presenting scientific information, we allow users to explore it, experiment with it, and learn through direct interaction.
We believe this matters because space science shouldn't be limited to researchers or specialists. By combining real scientific data, artificial intelligence, and interactive storytelling, we aim to inspire curiosity, encourage scientific thinking, and help the next generation connect with space exploration more engagingly.
details:
We used AI tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, to assist with code development, debugging, problem-solving, and refining parts of the project. All final decisions, design choices, testing, and project direction were reviewed and guided by our team.

1. What does our project do?

Moon Week is an interactive, educational space exploration game that puts players in charge of managing a lunar research base for seven consecutive mission days.

Players take the role of lunar mission decision-makers, responsible for keeping their crew and base operational while facing realistic challenges associated with living and working on the Moon.

Throughout the seven-day adventure, players encounter interconnected engineering and scientific challenges involving:

  • Lunar landing and site selection.
  • Water extraction and sustainable food production.
  • Energy generation, storage, and power management.
  • Lunar dust and extreme temperature management.
  • Solar radiation and astronaut protection.
  • Crew health, sleep cycles, and life-support systems.
  • Lunar rover exploration and communication systems.

The game is designed for children aged 7–12, making complex scientific concepts accessible through interactive gameplay and simplified scientific explanations.

2. How does the project work?

The experience is structured around seven connected chapters, each representing one mission day on the lunar base.

Players receive mission briefings, examine scientific information, interact with different base systems, and make decisions that affect their resources and crew.

The game uses interconnected resource-management mechanics, including:

  • Power and energy reserves.
  • Water and food supplies.
  • Life-support capacity.
  • Radiation shielding.
  • Crew health, fatigue, and readiness.
  • Rover battery and scientific progress.

One of the most important mechanics is that decisions are not isolated. Choices made during earlier mission days influence later events, available resources, base conditions, crew reactions, and possible mission outcomes.

For example, choosing a location with better sunlight may improve solar energy production, while selecting a location closer to permanently shadowed regions may provide better access to water ice and natural shielding.

The experience concludes with four possible endings:

  1. Scientific Breakthrough.
  2. Mission Accomplished.
  3. Critical Survival.
  4. Safe Abort Rescue.

After completing the mission, players can use the interactive What-If Choice Simulator (AI advisor) in the Mission Debrief to reconsider decisions and explore alternative outcomes.

3. What benefits does our project provide?

Our project provides educational, scientific, and practical learning benefits:

  • Scientific Literacy: Introduces players to real scientific concepts related to lunar exploration, astronomy, physics, and engineering.
  • Critical Thinking: Encourages players to evaluate different solutions and understand their consequences.
  • Problem-Solving: Presents interconnected challenges that require players to balance limited resources and competing priorities.
  • Systems Thinking: Demonstrates how energy, water, food, radiation protection, and human health depend on one another.
  • Decision-Making: Teaches players that engineering decisions involve trade-offs rather than universally perfect solutions.
  • Accessibility: Translates complicated scientific information into understandable explanations and interactive activities.
  • Learning Through Experience: Allows players to discover scientific principles by experimenting with different strategies rather than simply memorizing facts.

4. What is the intended impact of our project?

Our intended impact is to inspire younger generations to become more interested in space exploration, science, technology, and engineering.

We want children to understand that establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon is not simply about reaching another celestial body. It involves solving interconnected problems related to physics, biology, engineering, energy, environmental conditions, and human survival.

By allowing children to experience these challenges through gameplay, we aim to:

  • Make real space exploration challenges understandable and exciting.
  • Introduce children to NASA research and scientific discoveries.
  • Develop curiosity, analytical thinking, and engineering mindsets.
  • Demonstrate the importance of sustainability and responsible resource management.
  • Help young learners see themselves as future scientists, engineers, and space explorers.

Ultimately, we want to turn curiosity about the Moon into a deeper interest in understanding and exploring our universe.

5. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software did we use?

We developed Moon Week as a browser-based application using modern web technologies.

Programming Languages and Technologies:

  • TypeScript: Used for application logic, structured scientific data, and reliable game-state management.
  • HTML5: Provides the structure of the web application.
  • CSS3: Used for styling, visual effects, animations, and responsive layouts.
  • React 18: Used to build interactive interfaces and reusable components.
  • Tailwind CSS: Used for consistent styling and responsive interface design.
  • HTML5 Canvas: Used to render custom pixel-art graphics and interactive game environments.
  • Web Audio API: Used for procedural audio synthesis and interactive sound effects.

Libraries and Development Tools:

  • Vite: Development server and production build tool.
  • Lucide React: Open-source icon library.
  • Vitest: Used for automated testing.
  • Visual Studio Code: Primary development environment.
  • GitHub: Source-code hosting, version control, and team collaboration.

    (This point is not made by us; it is made by AI models.)

Scientific Data and External Resources:

  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).
  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) research.
  • NASA Artemis mission research.
  • NASA DONKI API for space weather observations.
  • NASA Human Research Program.
  • Canadian Space Agency educational research on space food production.

The application retrieves live solar flare information from NASA DONKI for relevant mission scenarios. It also includes verified, locally stored scientific reference data to maintain functionality when the external API is unavailable.

Hardware:

Development and testing were performed using standard personal computers. The final application runs through standard web browsers and does not require specialized hardware or external scientific equipment.

6. How is our project creative and innovative?

The central creative idea behind Moon Week is transforming lunar exploration into a continuous, decision-driven adventure rather than presenting scientific information as disconnected lessons.

We introduced several creative elements:

A Seven-Day Connected Narrative

The game follows a continuous mission story in which earlier decisions influence future chapters, character interactions, base conditions, and mission endings. This gives players a reason to think ahead rather than simply solve individual challenges.

Scientific Concepts Turned into Gameplay

Instead of explaining engineering concepts through text alone, we translate them into interactive simulations.

Our six hands-on lunar physics simulations cover:

  • Landing thrust and lunar descent.
  • Microgravity and capillary water movement.
  • Solar dust and electrical load balancing.
  • Solar flare radiation and proton shielding.
  • CO₂ scrubbing and circadian lighting.
  • Lunar rover and crater exploration.

Real NASA Research Integrated into Missions

Scientific observations and research studies are used as the foundation for mission challenges. Players encounter real concepts, measurements, and research references while making decisions inside the game.

Consequences and Multiple Endings

The four alternative endings make the experience more meaningful. Players can discover that a decision that initially appears beneficial may create difficulties later in the mission.

Interactive What-If Simulator

The Mission Debrief allows players to revisit their decisions and investigate how alternative choices could change the outcome. This encourages experimentation and reflection.

Original Pixel-Art Environment

We use a custom pixel-art visual style, interactive environments, animated elements, and procedural audio to create an engaging lunar adventure while keeping the application lightweight.

Our innovation is not simply putting scientific facts inside a game. It is connecting scientific research, interactive simulations, resource management, and narrative consequences into one coherent educational experience.

7. What factors did our team consider during development?

We considered several factors to ensure that the project would be scientifically meaningful, educational, accessible, and technically reliable.

Scientific Accuracy: We prioritized credible NASA and Canadian Space Agency research and distinguished between actual scientific observations and simplified gameplay representations.

Age Appropriateness: Since our intended audience is children aged 7–12, we simplified scientific terminology, used accessible explanations, and introduced concepts gradually without removing their scientific meaning.

Educational Value: Every major mission challenge was designed to teach or reinforce a scientific principle rather than exist solely for entertainment.

Realistic Engineering Trade-offs: We wanted players to understand that lunar missions involve competing priorities. For example, maximizing energy production may increase exposure to environmental hazards, while conserving resources may limit other operations.

Interconnected Gameplay: We designed the resource system and narrative progression so that decisions have consequences beyond the current mission day.

User Experience: We focused on intuitive navigation, understandable instructions, visual feedback, and a clear progression system.

Performance and Accessibility: We selected lightweight web technologies and custom graphical rendering techniques to avoid requiring powerful computers or specialized equipment.

Data Reliability: We considered network interruptions and API limitations by implementing locally stored verified scientific data as a fallback.

Scalability: We structured the application to support future missions, additional simulations, more scientific datasets, and expanded educational content.

8. What makes the project meaningful beyond entertainment?

Moon Week is designed to demonstrate that scientific education can be an active experience.

Players are not simply told how a lunar base works. They are placed in situations where they must think about how its systems interact, evaluate available information, and make decisions under constraints.

A choice about food production can affect electricity consumption. A decision about landing location can influence water accessibility and radiation protection. Crew fatigue can affect mission readiness. Communication failures can force astronauts to operate independently.

These relationships help players understand that successful space exploration depends on cooperation between different scientific and engineering disciplines, and the understanding of the importance of cooperation in general

Our Vision

We believe that the next generation of space explorers should not only learn about humanity's achievements in space but also understand the challenges that make those achievements possible.

Through Moon Week, we aim to make the experience of planning, managing, and sustaining a lunar mission accessible to young learners, and also make the experience of playing and engaging while studying astronomy achievable.

Our goal is to teach children about astronomy without boring study methods, but with an engaging educational approach, turning them into active problem-solvers and helping them imagine themselves contributing to the future of space exploration.
